from Pia Arke's exhibition Arctic Hysteria at Greenland's National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010 i. I am in my body. I am here, in front of you. I am the temperature in this room. I am undressed in my nudity; I am the light and shade you feel. I am more like other people than like you. I have before and after. I am my self, entirely and only. My outside and inside are continuous. I am muscle, organ, fluid, bone. I am monumental. You are the only one who sees me. ii. I am not naked as I am; I am naked as you see me. I am transparent, almost visible. I have a time and a place. I am tribal and exotic. I must always carry objects. You are heroic. I am a complete museum, the story of my own making. I am a mirror to you; you are reflected in the looking at me. At best, I mimic you. You write me. When you leave, I will no longer exist. iii. I am a single conscious point. I am indifferent. I am unself, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, before definition. Your body falls over me. I have depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I have infinite extension. I live inside the lived world, the light and dark inside my head like dream substance. I am camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker asserts a complete, embodied selfhood grounded in physical presence, continuity, and materiality.
- The speaker’s nakedness and identity are shaped by the viewer’s gaze rather than existing independently of it.
- Colonial and ethnographic perceptions reduce the speaker to something tribal, exotic, object-laden, and museum-like.
- The viewer creates and interprets the speaker as a reflection or imitation, making her existence dependent on being observed.
- The speaker ultimately becomes an indeterminate, expansive consciousness that inhabits light, darkness, dreams, and the room itself while both adoring and resisting the gaze.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Pia Arke’s *Arctic Hysteria* explores embodied identity, colonial spectatorship, and representation through a shifting first-person voice that moves from autonomous physical presence to exoticized museum object and finally to an ambiguous, camera-like consciousness. The work reveals how the observed Indigenous body is simultaneously constructed by, reflective of, and resistant to the viewer’s gaze, underscoring the unstable relationship between selfhood, colonial power, and visual representation.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Pia, Arke, Arctic

outputs.L1:
*From Pia Arke’s exhibition* Arctic Hysteria, *at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010*

**i.**  
I am in my body. I am here, before you. I am the temperature of this room. I am undressed in my nudity; I am the light and shadow you feel. I am more like other people than I am like you. I have a before and an after. I am myself, wholly and solely. My exterior and interior are continuous. I am muscle, organ, fluid, and bone. I am monumental. You are the only one who sees me.

**ii.**  
I am not naked as I am; I am naked as you see me. I am transparent, almost visible. I have a time and a place. I am tribal and exotic. I must always carry objects. You are heroic. I am a complete museum, the story of my own making. I am a mirror to you; you are reflected in the act of looking at me. At best, I mimic you. You write me. When you leave, I will cease to exist.

**iii.**  
I am a single, conscious point. I am indifferent. I am unself, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, preceding definition. Your body falls over me. I possess depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I extend infinitely. I live within the lived world, the light and darkness inside my head like dream substance. I am a camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.
outputs.L2:
*From Pia Arke’s 2010 exhibition* Arctic Hysteria, *presented at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives in Nuuk*

**i.**  
I inhabit my flesh. I stand here before you, equal to the warmth of this room. My bare body is uncovered; I become the brightness and shadow that touch you. I resemble humanity more than I resemble you. A past lies behind me and a future ahead. I belong wholly and exclusively to myself. No boundary separates my interior from my surface. I consist of muscles, organs, liquids, and bones. My presence is immense. No one sees me except you.

**ii.**  
My nakedness does not arise from what I am, but from the way you look at me. I am see-through, yet barely perceptible. I occupy a particular moment and location. I am cast as primitive and foreign. I am required to remain accompanied by things. You assume the heroic role. I contain an entire museum within me, including the account of how I came into being. I return your image: your act of observing me reveals you. The most I can do is imitate you. You author my existence. Once you depart, I disappear.

**iii.**  
I am one solitary center of awareness. Nothing concerns me. I exist without a self, resembling a photogram. I come from a time before history and before anything was named. Your physical form collapses across mine. I possess dimension and radiance. I belong to no fixed place, extending without limit. I dwell within the world as it is experienced, while brightness and darkness move through my mind like the material of dreams. I am both the camera obscura and the chamber containing it. I feel devotion and defiance at once.
outputs.L3:
The speaker initially asserts a complete and embodied sense of self, rooted in physical presence, continuity, and material existence. Her identity is not abstract or fragmented; it is grounded in the body and in the conviction that she occupies space as a whole, enduring being. Yet this selfhood is complicated by the viewer’s gaze. Her nakedness does not exist as a purely private or independent condition but is produced and defined through the act of being seen. In this sense, the viewer’s perception determines how her body is interpreted and, consequently, how her identity takes shape.

The gaze is also informed by colonial and ethnographic assumptions. Rather than recognizing the speaker as a self-determining subject, the viewer reduces her to an exotic or “tribal” figure associated with objects, artifacts, and museum displays. She is treated as something to be classified, exhibited, and interpreted. This process strips her body of its individual complexity and turns it into a cultural object, reproducing the distancing and dehumanizing logic of colonial observation.

As a result, the speaker’s existence becomes entangled with the viewer’s power to create meaning. She appears as a reflection, imitation, or projection fashioned by the person who observes her. Her identity seems dependent on visibility: she exists in the form the gaze gives her, even as she remains conscious of and resistant to that construction. By the end, however, she exceeds the fixed categories imposed upon her. She becomes an indeterminate and expansive consciousness inhabiting light and darkness, dreams and physical space, even the room itself. In this transformed state, she both adores the gaze for the recognition it offers and resists its attempt to define and contain her.
outputs.L4:
Pia Arke’s *Arctic Hysteria* examines the relationship between embodied identity, colonial spectatorship, and visual representation. Arke, a Greenlandic-Danish artist whose work repeatedly confronted the histories of Danish colonialism in Greenland, places the body at the center of this inquiry. The first-person voice associated with the work does not remain fixed or secure. Instead, it moves through several positions: an autonomous physical presence, an exoticized object of ethnographic display, and finally an ambiguous consciousness that appears to merge with the camera itself. Through these shifts, Arke demonstrates that identity is not simply expressed from within but is also produced through the visual and institutional structures that determine who may look, who must be seen, and how the seen body is interpreted.

At first, the speaking subject appears to inhabit her body directly. Her presence is physical, active, and self-aware rather than passive. This emphasis on embodiment resists the abstraction typical of colonial representation, in which Indigenous people are often reduced to examples of a racial or cultural category. Arke’s body cannot be separated from its movement, vulnerability, and material existence. It occupies space on its own terms and asserts a form of agency that precedes the viewer’s attempt to classify it. The first-person perspective initially suggests ownership: the body belongs to the speaker, and the speaker appears capable of determining what that body means.

Yet this autonomy quickly becomes unstable. Under the pressure of the viewer’s gaze, the body is transformed into an object to be examined. It begins to resemble an artifact in a museum or a specimen in an ethnographic collection—something displayed, categorized, and interpreted by others. This transformation invokes the historical role of museums, photography, anthropology, and other institutions in constructing colonial knowledge about Indigenous peoples. Such institutions did not merely preserve neutral evidence. They selected, arranged, labeled, and framed their subjects according to European expectations. The Indigenous body was made legible as “primitive,” “exotic,” or culturally authentic, while the authority of the observer remained largely invisible.

The title *Arctic Hysteria* intensifies this critique. “Hysteria” evokes a diagnostic language historically used to define certain bodies—especially female bodies—as irrational, unstable, or pathological. Combined with “Arctic,” the term suggests the colonial tendency to treat both Indigenous people and the northern environment as strange, excessive, and fundamentally different from European norms. The title therefore does not simply name a condition. It exposes the gaze that invents the condition and then claims the authority to diagnose it. What appears to be a description of the observed subject is also evidence of the observer’s assumptions, desires, and anxieties.

Arke complicates this dynamic by refusing to present the observed body as wholly powerless. Although the body is subjected to classification and display, it remains active within the image. It confronts, reflects, and unsettles the gaze directed toward it. The viewer may try to interpret the body through familiar colonial categories, but the work makes that interpretive process visible and uncomfortable. The spectator is no longer able to occupy a neutral position outside the scene. Looking becomes an implicated act. The meaning of the body emerges not from the body alone, but from the encounter between performer, image, camera, and audience.

The final shift toward a camera-like consciousness makes the relationship between subject and object even more ambiguous. The first-person voice no longer belongs securely to the person being observed. It seems to pass into the apparatus of representation itself, as though the camera has become a perceiving or speaking subject. This movement disrupts the conventional division between the person who looks and the person who is looked at. If the speaker can occupy both sides of the camera, then the colonial visual order is no longer stable. The represented subject may appropriate the technologies historically used to objectify her, turning them into instruments of reflection and critique.

At the same time, this shift does not offer a simple escape from colonial power. The camera remains connected to histories of surveillance, ethnographic documentation, and possession. To enter its perspective is therefore both empowering and dangerous. It may allow the subject to control representation, but it may also reveal how deeply the colonial gaze has shaped the subject’s own ways of seeing. Arke’s work refuses to resolve this contradiction. Instead, it shows identity as something formed through continual negotiation among bodily experience, inherited images, institutional categories, and acts of self-representation.

*Arctic Hysteria* ultimately presents vision as a contested field rather than a transparent means of knowing. The Indigenous body in the work is constructed by the viewer’s gaze because it is interpreted through colonial histories and visual conventions. It is reflective of that gaze because it reveals the fantasies and power structures projected onto it. Yet it also resists the gaze by remaining active, excessive, and impossible to contain within a single definition. Through its shifting first-person perspective, the work undermines any stable distinction between self and image, observer and observed, or agency and objectification. Arke thereby exposes representation not as a passive mirror of identity, but as a site where selfhood and colonial power are continually produced, challenged, and transformed.
outputs.L5:
Pia stood at the edge of the Arctic, where the horizon dissolved into snow and pale blue light. Beside her was Arke, a weathered research vessel built to cross frozen seas and withstand powerful winter storms.

Their journey was not only an expedition but also a search for understanding. As Arke moved quietly between towering icebergs, Pia recorded the sounds of cracking ice, the movement of wildlife, and the changing temperature of the ocean. The Arctic seemed endless and silent, yet every detail revealed a fragile world in motion.

Under the glow of the northern lights, Pia realized that Arke had carried her far beyond familiar maps. It had brought her to a place where nature spoke clearly—if people were willing to listen.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a three-part poetic meditation inspired by Pia Arke’s 2010 exhibition *Arctic Hysteria* at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives in Nuuk, exploring embodiment, the colonial gaze, museum display, photography, and resistance.
counterfactuals.output:
### I. The Body Is Not an Empty Country

First they named the land  
as if naming were a kind of arrival.  
Then they named the trembling body—  
*Arctic hysteria*—  
and wrote the words in a language  
that mistook its own fear for knowledge.

But the body beneath the fur,  
beneath the diagnosis,  
beneath the long white weather of the page,  
was never blank.

It carried salt, ancestry, lamp smoke,  
the muscle-memory of routes  
no compass had discovered.  
It knew that snow is not one color,  
that silence is crowded,  
that a woman watched  
is not therefore understood.

She lies across the map  
and the map becomes uncertain:  
coastlines enter the shoulder,  
mountains rise through breath,  
the measuring grid buckles  
under the warmth of her weight.

Who, now, is the territory?  
Who is lost?


### II. Museum Light

In the museum, everything is held  
at a careful distance:

the beadwork,  
the blade,  
the photograph whose subject  
has outlived the photographer’s caption.

Glass makes a second climate—  
still, bright, obedient.  
Inside it, objects are taught  
to stop moving.

Yet hide remembers the animal.  
Wood remembers the hand.  
A camera remembers  
who stood behind it,  
who was told to stand still,  
who refused by looking back.

Across the floor, colonial history  
arranges its evidence:  
label, date, donor, expedition.  
A whole people reduced  
to provenance.

But the photograph has a dark interior.  
Enter it and you hear  
the shutter’s small metallic command;  
remain, and you hear another sound—  
breath continuing beyond the frame.

The archive says: *This was.*  
The body answers: *I am not finished.*


### III. Exposure / Resistance

Let resistance begin  
not as a monument  
but as a change in posture.

A hand touches the image.  
A naked body occupies the chart.  
The lens, once aimed like a weapon,  
is made to confess its angle.

There is no innocent looking.  
There is only the choice  
to meet the gaze  
or hide inside it.

Nuuk gathers the exhibition  
into rooms of snowlight and shadow.  
Outside, the city speaks in windows,  
harbor water, engines, children—  
a present tense no vitrine can contain.

And she returns, not as specimen,  
not as symptom,  
not as the beautiful proof  
of someone else’s North,

but as interruption:

skin against paper,  
laughter against taxonomy,  
memory against the clean white wall.

The map does not disappear.  
The museum does not fall.  
The photograph keeps its wound.

Still, from within the image,  
a figure rises—  
bearing every name forced upon her,  
and every name withheld—

then turns toward us  
with the fierce composure  
of one who knows:

to be seen is not surrender;  
to look back  
is to alter the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem in three numbered sections from the perspective of an Indigenous female body being viewed in a museum. Move from physical self-presence, to exoticization by the spectator, to an abstract camera-obscura-like consciousness.
counterfactuals.output:
**1. BODY, PRESENT TENSE**

I am not the past tense they printed beside me.  
My shoulder remembers weather. My mouth keeps  
the red syllable of my nation behind its teeth.  
Even here, under museum light, my blood moves—  
small rivers refusing the map.

Glass does not make me still.  
I feel each footstep enter the floor,  
each breath cloud and vanish.  
My hands, arranged by another hand, dream  
their old work: braid, paddle, cradle, strike.  
I am wholly inside my skin.  
I am not inside your label.

**2. SPECIMEN / SPECTACLE**

You arrive wearing the soft authority of looking.  
Your eyes inventory: bead, bone, breast, scar.  
You call me *exquisite*, meaning distant.  
You call me *tragic*, meaning finished.

Behind you, the gift shop multiplies me—  
my face on paper, my pattern made purchasable,  
a feather where no feather belongs.  
You lean closer. The glass returns your hunger  
as education.

I become your beautiful elsewhere,  
your proof that the world was once wild  
before you named it. But listen:  
the exotic is only your own reflection  
dressed in what you took from me.

**3. CAMERA OBSCURA**

Now the chamber darkens. A pinhole opens  
somewhere beyond the building.

Light enters backward.

The museum turns upside down inside my skull:  
visitors walk the ceiling; captions sink into air;  
the curator becomes a small inverted shadow  
crossing the field of my attention.

I am no longer object, nor eye,  
but the black room where seeing happens—  
image without possession, aperture without frame.  
Ancestors flare across the inner wall,  
not ghosts but wavelengths.

The body dissolves into a lens of night.  
The lens remembers nothing by holding it.  
The lens remembers by letting light pass through,  
altered, reversed, alive—  
and outside, an unnamed world  
continues entering me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Respond ekphrastically to Pia Arke’s *Arctic Hysteria* using repeated first-person declarations beginning with “I am.” Contrast nakedness with being made naked by another’s gaze, and include themes of transparency, mimicry, photographic space, and colonial representation.
counterfactuals.output:
I am. Naked by my own arrival, skin entering the room before history can dress me.

I am. Made naked when your gaze names my body evidence, symptom, native, absence.

I am. A figure moving across photographic snow, though the snow is paper and the paper remembers who framed it.

I am. Transparent only because the image demands to see through me—to map coast, blood, weather, ancestry beneath my skin.

I am. Opaque where I refuse.

I am. Mimicking the posture you expect: the Arctic woman seized by hysteria, the colonial specimen performing the caption written in advance.

I am. Mimicking badly, deliberately, until imitation becomes disturbance.

I am. Crawling through photographic space, where distance is flattened and every horizon belongs to the camera.

I am. Pressing my body against the landscape that representation has made empty.

I am. Naked, and nakedness is mine: breath, muscle, exposure, choice.

I am. Made naked, and that nakedness is yours: classification, possession, the cold aperture of looking.

I am. Tearing the image because it will not open.

I am. Opening it by force.

I am. Both body and blur, daughter and double, subject and wound in the emulsion.

I am. Not the Arctic you imagined.

I am. The movement that makes your photograph fail.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical exhibition text for “Pia Arke’s exhibition Arctic Hysteria at Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010.” Structure it as i., ii., and iii., addressing the viewer directly and examining body, museum, image, time, and identity.
counterfactuals.output:
**i.**

You enter with your body before you enter with your name.  
Your breath meets the museum’s measured air; your footsteps cross floors where objects have been taught to wait. Here, in *Arctic Hysteria*, the body is neither evidence nor ornament. It is weather. It presses against the image, inhabits it, disturbs its claim to distance.

Pia Arke places herself where the landscape was once expected to be empty. She bends, blurs, exposes, returns. Her body interrupts the colonial view—the Arctic as horizon, resource, silence—and makes looking physical again. You do not stand outside these images. You are implicated in their frame.

What has been called hysteria may also be knowledge without permission: a body remembering what official language cannot contain.

**ii.**

You are inside Greenland’s National Museum & Archives, but the museum is also inside the work: its inventories, omissions, labels, and inherited ways of seeing. Around you, photographs carry the double life of documents. They appear to preserve, yet they also cut, arrange, and possess.

Ask each image: Who stood behind the camera? Who was made visible? Who was asked to disappear?

Arke’s images do not answer cleanly. They reopen the archive as a wound and a workshop. Maps become skins; landscapes become rooms; family photographs drift between private memory and public history. The museum no longer seems like a shelter from time. It becomes a tide line where things taken, saved, forgotten, and returned gather together.

You look at the past, and the past alters your gaze.

**iii.**

Time here does not move forward. It folds. 2010 touches childhood; colonial history touches the present tense; the dead remain active in the image. A photograph says *this has been*, but Arke makes it ask: *What is still happening?*

Identity, too, refuses the straight line. It is not a choice between Greenlandic and Danish, self and other, belonging and exile. It is the unsettled space between names—a geography carried in the body, revised by memory, sharpened by loss.

As you leave, do not search for a single portrait of Pia Arke, or of Greenland, or of yourself. Notice instead what trembles at the edges: the cropped figure, the damaged surface, the place where body and landscape exchange their boundaries.

You came to view an exhibition.  
Now the images are viewing you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, philosophical prose poem influenced by phenomenology and postcolonial art criticism. Let a photographed body speak to “you,” first asserting its material reality, then describing how spectators construct it as tribal and exotic, and finally dissolving into light, depth, dream, and camera obscura.
counterfactuals.output:
I am not the emblem you found waiting in the silver salts. I was weight before I was image: heel against dust, pulse under the tongue, sweat cooling in the hinge of the knee. My skin did not begin where your looking began. It held weather, labor, the small archives of touch; it resisted the sun, entered water, healed badly, desired. You call me body because the frame has taught you where to stop.

Then you arrive with your educated hunger. Around my wrist you fasten “tribe,” over my shoulders you drape “origin,” in my gaze you plant the dark flower of the exotic. You praise my authenticity until I can no longer move. Every ornament becomes evidence; every scar, a border; every silence, an ancestral speech translated by your caption. You make distance into beauty and beauty into innocence, forgetting the lens traveled with the gun, the ledger, the museum case. You say I am timeless because you have removed the clocks.

But look longer: I am already escaping your grammar. The outline loosens. My face becomes an aperture through which depth remembers it was never empty. Light crosses me without permission, breaks into grain, reverses the world. I fall backward into the black chamber where seeing is born upside down. There, neither subject nor specimen, I am the interval between flame and wall, a dream developing in its own darkness. You reach for me and touch only radiance—then shadow—then the immeasurable interior of your own eye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
